steps.label: Conclusion (Clearly)
steps.body: Smith's proposed ordinance does not even merit consideration.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Smith is now proposing an ordinance that bans the "bait-and-switch" sales tactic. But four years ago, Smith owned an appliance store that was famous for its use of bait-and-switch.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Whenever a Flaw argument rejects someone's proposal, ask what the rejection is based on. Is it the proposal itself, or the person who made it?

The council president never says a word about the ordinance. Would it work? Would it protect shoppers? Is bait-and-switch harmful? None of that comes up. The only reason given is Smith's past: Smith's store was famous for the very tactic the ordinance would ban.

That is the Ad Hominem flaw: dismissing a position because of its source rather than its content. Smith's history might make Smith look like a hypocrite, but hypocrisy doesn't make an idea bad. Given that Smith once used bait-and-switch, how could we still argue the ordinance deserves a hearing? Easily. People change. Smith may have watched customers get burned and now wants the tactic gone. Someone who knows a tactic from the inside may even be well placed to write a rule against it.

Notice what the president does not say. The president never claims the ordinance is false or mistaken, only that it "does not even merit consideration." So answers about proving a claim false miss the target. The objection is to refusing to look at the ordinance at all.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer describing this famous flaw; often it sounds like "the author dismisses an argument because of its source rather than its content". Otherwise, it might be a more specific answer that says, "because Person X did thing A in the past, we shouldn't listen to X's idea to do away with thing A."

notes.body: This is the prediction almost word for word. The "source" is Smith, the person who proposed the ordinance, and the president's only reason is Smith's old store. The "content" is what the ordinance would actually do, which the president never discusses. Test it: could the ordinance still be a good law even though Smith once used bait-and-switch? Yes. So the president's reason never touches the ordinance. When every reason for rejecting an idea is about the person behind it, look for this source-versus-content wording.

A single fact that truly contradicts a claim does show the claim is false, so this often isn't even a flaw. And the president never says the ordinance is false. Smith's old store is not incompatible with the ordinance being a good law; it is a fact about the person who wrote it.

The president never discusses sales tactics at all, deceptive or legitimate. Nothing in the argument depends on what counts as bait-and-switch, so no distinction between kinds of tactics is needed. The argument fails because it looks only at who proposed the ordinance.

Circular reasoning would mean the premise already states the conclusion. The premise is about Smith's store four years ago; the conclusion is that the ordinance does not merit consideration. Those are different claims. The premise is about the wrong thing, but it doesn't repeat the conclusion.

There is no generalization here. The president moves from one fact about Smith to one conclusion about Smith's ordinance and never extends the point to other councilmembers, other ordinances, or bait-and-switch in general. With no sample and no broader category, a generalization flaw has nothing to describe.

why: Evaluate used a gendered pronoun for the council president and dash-style definitions, Evidence used a gendered pronoun for Smith, and all five notes were long em-dash-register paragraphs that repeated the same point.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
Great works of art evoke passionate responses in those who view them.
GW → PR

The work of abstract painter Ezekiel Reilly elicits intensely emotional responses in those who view it.
Reilly's art: PR

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body:
Reilly's art is great.
Reilly's art: GW

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The first premise is a conditional. If a work is great, then it evokes passionate responses. That makes a passionate response necessary for greatness: every great work has one.

The evidence tells us Reilly's work has the passionate response. Then the conclusion jumps to greatness. That runs the arrow backward:

Premise: GW → PR
Author's move: PR, so GW

In order to draw this conclusion, we must assume that any work of art which elicits a passionate response is a great work. That is an illegal reversal of the first premise. The rule tells us what follows from being great. It says nothing about what follows from stirring up strong feelings.

Think of a painting viewers find offensive, or a clumsy portrait that makes people furious. Both provoke intense reactions without being great art. A passionate response is a requirement for greatness, not proof of it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for the classic necessary vs. sufficient answer: the argument treats something required for greatness (a passionate response) as if it were enough for greatness. A conversational version would say the argument fails to consider that a work can evoke passionate responses without being great.

notes.body: Circular reasoning would mean a premise already assumes Reilly's art is great. Neither premise does. One is a general rule about great art; the other reports how viewers react to Reilly's work. The conclusion adds something new. The trouble is the direction the rule is applied in, not a premise that assumes the answer.

This is the prediction in formal language. "A condition that is necessary for having a certain quality" is evoking passionate responses, which every great work must do. "As if it must also be sufficient" is the author's move: Reilly's work has the passionate response, so it must be great. Check it by plugging in the terms: did the author treat a passionate response as enough for greatness? Yes, that is the whole argument. Whenever a Flaw argument gives you "if X, then Y," shows Y, and concludes X, look for this answer.

For C to fit, Reilly's work would need to be an unusual case that the general claim doesn't really cover. Nothing suggests that. The rule about great art isn't misapplied to an odd case; it is run backward. Even if Reilly were a perfectly typical painter, the reversal would still be a flaw.

A hasty generalization builds a broad claim from a small sample. The argument's general claim, that great works evoke passionate responses, is offered as a premise, not drawn from examples. The conclusion is about one painter's work. No sample, no generalization to criticize.

Check the premises for value language. The first premise is about great works of art, and "great" is the same value judgment the conclusion makes about Reilly. So the argument does start from a premise involving values. E describes a gap this argument does not have.

why: Diagrams were inline, the stimulus person was referred to with a gendered pronoun, there was no Goal step, and every note was a long em-dash paragraph restating the same reversal point.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Voice mail will soon make answering machines obsolete.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Voice mail does the same job as an answering machine and is more convenient, more flexible, and cheaper.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The companies predict that answering machines will become obsolete, meaning hardly anyone will keep using them. Their reason is a list of voice mail's strengths: more convenient, more flexible, less expensive.

Given that voice mail beats answering machines on all three, how could we argue answering machines will still survive? The list only covers what voice mail is good at. It never asks whether answering machines do something voice mail can't. If they offer one valuable feature voice mail lacks, some customers will keep their machines for that feature alone, and the machines won't become obsolete.

Notice how strong the conclusion is: "obsolete." To weaken it, we don't have to show answering machines will win. We only need a reason a meaningful number of people would keep using them.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an advantage answering machines have that voice mail does not offer, something useful enough that people would keep their machines for it. Answers that add more voice mail strengths, or more answering machine weaknesses, help the companies instead.

notes.body: A says every call to a voice-mail subscriber goes through, even when the line is busy, which answering machines cannot match. That is one more advantage for voice mail, so it strengthens the companies' argument instead of calling it into question.

B tells us when answering machine sales surged: right after they first came out. Past sales say nothing about whether voice mail is better than answering machines now, so B has no effect on the prediction that answering machines will become obsolete.

Being able to cancel voice mail at any time makes the service more flexible and less risky to try. If anything, that helps voice mail win customers, which fits the companies' argument rather than undercutting it.

This is the missing advantage we predicted. With an answering machine, you can hear who is calling and then decide whether to pick up. Voice mail can't do that. Anyone who likes screening calls now has a reason to keep a machine even if voice mail is cheaper and more convenient, so the machines may not become obsolete. When an argument predicts that a new option will replace an old one, look for a benefit the old option keeps that the new one lacks.

E points out a limit of answering machines: the tape caps how many messages they can record. A weakness of answering machines makes it more likely that voice mail replaces them, so E supports the argument, if anything.

why: Evaluate only restated the gap without building the objection, the Goal named the task loosely, and the correct-answer note was a single 9-word verdict.

steps.label: Statements
steps.body: Technology could raise food production, but only negligibly unless societies centralize. Historically, the more centralized a society, the more of its people died when it collapsed. So centralizing to boost food production will make collapses worse.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Pause and infer before reading the choices. Line up the two relationships:

Better technology → more food, but only a negligible increase without centralization
More centralization → a greater share of people perish if the society collapses

So the technology route to more food runs through centralization, and centralization makes collapse deadlier. That is why the author concludes the effort will "merely exacerbate the disasters associated with societal collapse."

What does that tell us about technology and collapse? If better technology could prevent every problem that comes with a collapse, the author couldn't say the technology-driven plan only makes those disasters worse. So at least one collapse problem, the higher death toll, is something technology does not fix.

On Most Strongly Supported questions, a weakly worded answer like "not every" is easy to prove. It needs only one exception, and the stimulus hands us one.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Technology won't prevent every problem that comes with a centralized society's collapse. Look for a modestly worded answer along those lines. Be wary of answers that claim a trend over time, an "only" relationship, or anything about population growth the passage never addresses.

notes.body: The passage links centralization to one thing: how many people perish when a society collapses. It never says centralized societies need more food. The link it does give runs the other way: the push for more food is the reason to centralize. A reverses that, making centralization the cause of a greater need for food.

B asks for very little. "Not every" problem means at least one problem survives the technology. The passage supplies one: the technology route to more food requires centralization, and centralization makes collapse deadlier. Technology doesn't prevent that higher death toll; the author says the effort makes it worse. When an answer is this modestly worded, check whether the stimulus gives you one clear case. Here it does.

The passage says populations will increase, but nothing about the rate of growth, let alone a rate that keeps rising forever. "Continue to increase indefinitely" is a claim about the future that no statement here supports.

The passage says technology will enable food production to increase. It never says technology is the only way to do it. If anything, it stresses centralization as a requirement for meaningful increases. To support "only by improved technology," we would need to rule out every other route, and nothing does.

The passage's history covers one relationship: more centralized societies lost a greater share of their people when they collapsed. It never says societies became more centralized as technology improved. The centralization it discusses is something societies would have to undertake, not a trend it reports.

why: Evaluate did not show why the stimulus proves the weak claim, the A note made an unverified popularity claim, and the C, D and E notes were one-line verdicts without a reason tied to the passage.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: The ancient Egyptians were the first society to produce alcoholic beverages.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: An Egyptian cup dating from 2000 B.C. depicts what appears to be a brewery, and its chemical residue shows it held alcoholic beer. That is older than the Babylonian wine-making evidence from 1500 B.C., which had been thought to be the first.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
"First known" and "first ever" are different claims. The cup is the earliest evidence of alcohol we have found. That puts Egypt ahead of Babylon on the evidence so far, but the conclusion says the Egyptians were the first society to produce alcoholic beverages at all.

Given the 2000 B.C. cup, how could we argue the Egyptians were not first? Another society could have brewed or fermented something earlier and left no trace, or left one nobody has dug up yet. The argument even shows how this happens: the Babylonians were thought to be first until this cup turned up. The next discovery could do the same to the Egyptians.

Whenever a conclusion says something was the first, the only, or never happened, check whether the evidence covers everything or just what has been found so far.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Find an answer that points out the gap between "earliest evidence we have" and "first ever."

notes.body: A generalization flaw would need a claim about Egyptian society as a whole, such as how common beer drinking was. The conclusion isn't about that. One cup is enough to show alcohol was being made in Egypt by 2000 B.C. The real question is whether anyone made it before then.

The term holds steady. The premises mention Babylonian wine and Egyptian beer, and the conclusion's "alcoholic beverages" covers both in the same sense. Nothing shifts meaning between premises and conclusion. The argument compares dates, so the weak spot is about what came first, not what the words mean.

The argument never says Babylonian wine-making depended on Egyptian brewing. It claims only that Egypt came first in time. C describes a claim about one society's technology depending on another's, and the author makes no such claim, so there is nothing for this criticism to attack.

This is the gap we predicted. "The first known instance of a kind" is the 2000 B.C. Egyptian cup, the oldest evidence found so far. "The first instance of that kind" is what the conclusion claims: the Egyptians were the first society ever to produce alcohol. The author treats the two as the same. Test it: could some society have made alcohol before 2000 B.C. without leaving evidence we have found? Yes, and the Babylonians losing their title shows new finds can overturn an old first. When a Flaw conclusion claims a first, look for this answer.

Arguments may state background facts without proving them, and the 1500 B.C. date mainly tells us what used to be believed. Supporting it wouldn't help the argument anyway: even a well-documented Babylonian date can't show that no society produced alcohol before 2000 B.C. The flaw is elsewhere.

why: Evidence and Evaluate used em dashes and Evaluate did not build the objection or state the reusable check; the notes were thin, and the correct-answer note did not teach how to spot the first-known vs first-ever gap.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
Political candidates' speeches are loaded with promises and with expressions of good intention.

But one must not forget that the politicians' purpose in giving these speeches is to get themselves elected.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Clearly, then, these speeches are selfishly motivated and the promises made in them are unreliable.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The evidence is about motive: candidates give speeches to get elected. The conclusion has two parts. The first, that the speeches are selfishly motivated, follows closely from that motive. The second is the leap: the promises are unreliable.

Why would a selfish motive make a promise unreliable? The author never says. This is an attack on the source rather than the content. The reason someone has for saying something doesn't tell us whether it is true or whether it will be kept.

Given that candidates make promises to get elected, how could we argue the promises are still reliable? A candidate who wants to win the next election also has a selfish reason to keep them, since broken promises cost votes. The motive might even make the promises more reliable. Either way, an ulterior motive alone doesn't settle whether a promise can be trusted.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the argument overlooks that a promise made for a self-interested reason can still be reliable. In formal terms: it rejects the promises because of the speaker's motive rather than because of any evidence about the promises themselves.

notes.body: The argument assumes that a selfishly motivated promise is unreliable. A flips that into its negation: a promise that is not selfishly motivated is reliable. The argument never needs that. It says nothing about unselfish promises at all, so it isn't presuming anything about them.

"Never kept" is far stronger than "unreliable." An unreliable promise is one we can't count on; it might still be kept some of the time. The argument only needs selfish promises to be untrustworthy, not broken every time, so it doesn't presume what B describes.

Confusing cause and effect would mean treating a result as if it were the reason. The argument doesn't do that. It names the candidates' purpose, getting elected, as the motive behind the speeches, which is exactly what a purpose is. The flaw is the jump from that motive to unreliable promises.

This matches the prediction. The "ulterior motive" is the candidates' purpose of getting elected, and "a promise need not be unreliable" denies the second half of the conclusion. The argument moves from why a promise was made to whether it can be trusted, and D points out that the first doesn't settle the second. Whenever an argument rejects a claim because of the speaker's motives, look for an answer that separates the motive from the merit of what was said.

Whether a candidate is worthy of office is a different issue. The argument concludes only that the speeches are selfishly motivated and the promises unreliable, so a criticism about the candidate's worthiness misses what the argument claims.

why: The Conclusion and Evaluate steps were fused into the Evidence body, there was no Goal, Evaluate was one line, and the A, B and D notes were thin verdicts (D just said it correctly describes the difference).
